 The average Social Security benefit for 65-year-olds is $1,607.27 per month as of December 2025, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). This age is a major milestone for Medicare eligibility, but it's no longer the baseline for a full Social Security check. If you're 65 today, your full retirement age (FRA) is 67.
 Social Security calculates your benefit based on your average inflation-adjusted wages from your 35 highest-earning years. It's designed to replace about 40% of your pre-retirement income, which is well short of what most seniors actually need. Most people rely on savings or other income to fill the gap.
 Image source: Getty Images.
 What 65-year-olds collect
 The average monthly payment for men at age 65 is $1,772.00, while the average for women is $1,457.40. This reflects a gender gap of $314.60 per month. If your full retirement age is 67, claiming at 65 results in a permanent 13.33% early claiming benefit reduction.
 The table below breaks down these averages as of December 2025, the most recent data from the SSA.
 age overall men women 
 65 $1,607.27 $1,772.00 $1,457.40 
 The cost of claiming early
 Medicare eligibility at 65 doesn't mean you've reached full retirement age for Social Security. If you were born in 1960 or later, claiming at 65 is still considered early. You trade a smaller monthly benefit for the ability to receive income two years sooner.
 A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027, adding about $58 a month on top of the average age-65 benefit. These adjustments are designed to help your benefits keep up with inflation. However, they can change annually and don't always match your actual spending increases.
 Your ultimate benefit depends on your earnings history and the age you choose to start your payments.
 Why 65 is no longer full retirement age
 Many people believe that 65 represents the full retirement age (FRA) -- the age at which you qualify for your full Social Security benefit based on your work history -- because it used to. But changing demographics forced the government to push up the FRA over time.
 Back when Social Security was facing its last funding crisis in the 1980s, the government passed legislation mandating a gradual increase in the FRA from age 65 to age 67 over several decades. That transition will be complete in 2027.
 This move effectively amounted to a benefit cut for younger workers, who now face steeper early-claiming penalties than their older counterparts who claimed at the same age. This is something all seniors should weigh carefully when deciding which claiming age makes the most sense for them.
 If you choose to delay your Social Security application, you should still sign up for Medicare at age 65, though. Seniors who fail to do this can face lifetime premium penalties for applying for Medicare late.
 For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide .
